children: CEO Nikesh Arora is pushing back on calls for the technology industry to collectively slow AI development, arguing that competition makes coordinated restraint unrealistic. For Palo Alto investors, the debate has a direct business implication: if increasingly powerful AI systems keep arriving quickly, companies may need to spend more aggressively on cybersecurity to protect against attacks that are faster, cheaper and easier to scale.

Palo Alto Networks is one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies, selling software and services that protect corporate networks, cloud infrastructure and applications. Its growth increasingly depends on convincing customers to consolidate security spending onto its broader platform.
Speaking on CNBC's The Tech Download podcast, Arora said voluntary industry-wide restraint is unlikely to work.
I think not everybody is going to pace themselves, Arora said.
Instead, he put responsibility on individual developers.
Don't release your product if you don't believe it's going to be safe, Arora said.

That position broadly echoes Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's argument that companies should test AI systems rigorously and withhold products that fail safety standards, while differing from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's recent call for slower frontier-model development.

The debate is especially relevant for Palo Alto because AI is changing both sides of cybersecurity. Attackers can use models to automate and scale threats, while defenders can deploy AI to detect vulnerabilities and respond faster.

Palo Alto underscored that opportunity this week by launching Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, which uses multiple advanced AI models to continuously search for vulnerabilities in applications, APIs and cloud systems.
For PANW investors, the key question is whether faster AI adoption translates into faster security spending.

Investors should watch growth in AI-focused security products, platform adoption, remaining performance obligations and whether new services create incremental revenue rather than simply replacing existing tools.
The bullish setup is straightforward: rapidly advancing AI increases both enterprise productivity and the attack surface companies must defend.

The risk is that AI security becomes highly competitive or customers resist additional spending. Arora's comments do not alter Palo Alto's financial outlook by themselves, but they reinforce the premise that cybersecurity requirements may rise alongside AI capabilities.

title: Palo Alto CEO Sends Stark Signal on AI
